content.title: About
content.content: Beans with meat is a ready‑to‑eat dish consisting of boiled beans, stewed meat (usually beef or pork) and seasonings. It is a traditional staple in many cuisines, valued for its heartiness, rich flavor, and high protein content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans are one of the oldest cultivated legumes, grown for over 7,000 years.
Combining beans with meat provides a complete set of essential amino acids.
In many regions the dish is flavored with tomato paste, onion and spices for a distinctive aroma.
Dried beans can be stored for several years; the prepared dish keeps in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days.
Traditionally beans with meat are served with bread, rice or mashed potatoes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The combination of beans and meat delivers a high amount of both plant and animal protein, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Beans provide soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting digestive health and stabilizing blood sugar levels.

items.title: Provides iron and zinc
items.content: Meat and beans together supply iron and zinc, essential for immune function and energy metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains vitamin B6, niacin and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: May support heart health
items.content: Bean fiber and the moderate amount of healthy fats from meat can help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared versions often contain added salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Beans can cause gas in sensitive people; soaking before cooking reduces this effect.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Using low‑quality or undercooked meat carries a risk of food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve beans with meat hot as a main course. Garnish with fresh herbs, sour cream or a spicy sauce. It pairs well with boiled rice, mashed potatoes or fresh bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for 2‑3 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consumption.

beef-steak-t-bone-ns-as-to-fat-eaten.title: Beef, steak, T‑bone, no bone marrow

content.title: About
content.content: The T‑bone steak is a large cut of beef that includes a portion of the tenderloin and a portion of the strip loin, separated by a T‑shaped bone. It is prized for its rich beef flavor, moderate fat content, and the contrasting textures of the two muscles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: T‑bone steaks are considered one of the most “royal” cuts because of their juiciness and flavor.
The T‑shaped bone helps retain heat, resulting in more even cooking.
They are a staple on steak‑house menus, often grilled or oven‑roasted.
In the United States the same cut is called a “porterhouse” when the tenderloin side is larger, and “T‑bone” when it is smaller.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Heme iron from beef is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: T‑bone steak supplies B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals are important for immune function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: Naturally occurring creatine can help improve physical performance and maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise blood cholesterol levels.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked beef can harbor harmful bacteria such as E. coli or Salmonella.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rare, but some individuals may experience allergic reactions.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Large portions can increase uric acid, which is a concern for gout sufferers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Best cooked over high heat (grill, cast‑iron skillet) to the desired doneness, then rested 5‑10 minutes. Serve with vegetables, potatoes, or a light sauce. Slice the meat away from the bone before eating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging for 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen steak in the refrigerator before cooking.

chicken-wing-baked-broiled-or-roasted-fr.title: Chicken wing, baked, broiled, or roasted, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wings are the meat from the forelimbs of a chicken, commonly prepared by baking, broiling, or grilling. The raw product (856) is fresh, unprocessed wings ready for cooking. Wings have a tender flavor, juicy texture, and a distinctive aroma that intensifies with heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings are a staple of American cuisine, especially in the form of Buffalo wings.
They are traditionally served with blue‑cheese dressing and celery sticks.
Wings can be prepared in many ways: baked in the oven, grilled, or deep‑fried.
In the United States more than 1.5 billion servings of wings are consumed each year.
They are often marinated in soy, honey, or spicy sauces before cooking.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken wings provide high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Wings supply phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Ideal for low‑carb diets as they contain virtually no carbs.

items.title: Provides collagen
items.content: The skin and connective tissue are rich in collagen, beneficial for skin and joint health.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Wings, especially with skin, contain a notable amount of fat; excessive intake can contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Raw wings may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Prepared marinades are often high in salt; choose low‑sodium options if you have hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wings can be baked at 200 °C for 25‑30 minutes, grilled, or pan‑fried. Common marinades include soy sauce, honey, spices, or a simple salt‑and‑pepper rub. Serve hot with dipping sauces such as barbecue, hot sauce, or garlic butter, alongside celery or carrot sticks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw wings in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the refrigerator before cooking, never at room temperature.

coffee-iced-cafe-mocha-decaffeinated-non.title: Coffee, Iced Cafe Mocha, Decaf, Nonfat

content.title: About
content.content: Iced Cafe Mocha is a cold beverage made from espresso, chocolate syrup, and nonfat milk, prepared without caffeine. It combines the aromatic taste of coffee, the sweetness of chocolate, and a light creamy texture while keeping calories low.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first "mocha" originated in Yemen in the 15th century, where coffee was mixed with chocolate.
Decaffeination is usually done by water or CO₂ methods, preserving most flavor notes.
Nonfat milk contains about 90 % less fat but retains most of the protein and calcium.
Cold coffee drinks gained popularity in the US in the 1990s thanks to the rise of Starbucks.
Chocolate syrup is often made from cocoa mass, sugar, and vanilla, giving the drink its distinctive aroma.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Chocolate syrup provides flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Nonfat milk supplies calcium and vitamin D, beneficial for bones and heart.

items.title: Reduced caffeine intake
items.content: Decaf coffee lets you enjoy the flavor without the stimulant effect, useful for caffeine‑sensitive individuals.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Nonfat milk offers about 3 g of protein per 100 ml, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Chocolate can boost serotonin levels, helping improve mood.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein should choose dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Chocolate syrup adds sugar; those monitoring glucose should watch portion size.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Some brands use artificial flavors; check the ingredient list if you avoid additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Iced Cafe Mocha over ice in a glass. You can top with whipped cream, dust with cocoa powder, or swap regular chocolate syrup for a diet version.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared drink refrigerated in a sealed container for no more than 24 hours. Store nonfat milk at 0‑4 °C and keep chocolate syrup in a cool, dry place.

content.title: About
content.content: Decaffeinated latte is a beverage made from roasted coffee beans that have had most of their natural caffeine removed, mixed with nonfat milk and a flavoring agent. The nonfat milk provides a light, creamy texture without added fat, while the flavor (e.g., vanilla, caramel, or hazelnut) adds a pleasant taste note.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually done by water extraction or solvent methods before the beans are roasted.
Nonfat milk retains most of the protein but virtually no fat.
Flavored drinks often use natural extracts, though artificial flavors are also common.
Decaf latte is popular among caffeine‑sensitive individuals and those who enjoy coffee flavor in the evening.
In the United States, over 30 % of ready‑to‑drink coffee sales are decaffeinated varieties.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Nonfat milk supplies calcium and protein without the saturated fats found in whole‑milk beverages, supporting low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Antioxidant presence
items.content: Even without caffeine, coffee retains polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Certain flavorings such as ginger or cinnamon can aid digestion.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Nonfat milk provides about 300 mg of calcium per 250 ml serving, contributing to bone health.

items.title: Hydration aid
items.content: The drink is mostly water, helping meet daily fluid needs.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or lactose should choose dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Artificial flavor additives
items.content: Some artificial flavorings may trigger sensitivities in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Reduced mouthfeel
items.content: Lack of fat can make the beverage feel less rich compared to a traditional latte.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot or iced, add to coffee‑mocha drinks, use as a base for dessert sauces or smoothies. Sweeten with honey, stevia, or maple syrup if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1‑4 °C in a sealed container for up to 7 days after opening. Freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months; thaw in the refrigerator before use.

frozen-fruit-juice-bar-no-sugar-added.title: Frozen fruit juice bar, no sugar added

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen fruit juice bar is a frozen fruit snack made from 100 % natural fruit juices with no added sugar. It contains concentrated berry and tropical fruit juices and a small amount of natural stabilizers to maintain texture. The bar offers a refreshing taste, bright fruit notes, and is perfect for a quick snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bars are flash‑frozen right after forming, preserving most of the vitamins and antioxidants.
No added sugar makes them suitable for people monitoring blood glucose levels.
Each bar provides more than 30 % of the daily recommended vitamin C intake.
Only pectin, a plant‑based gelling agent, is used to stabilize the texture.
The product is free from gluten, dairy, and artificial flavors.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Fruit juices contain polyphenols and carotenoids that combat free radicals.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: The frozen product has a high water content, aiding overall hydration.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Absence of added sugar and presence of dietary fiber help stabilize blood sugar levels.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific fruits used in the formulation.

items.title: Cold product
items.content: The low temperature may cause discomfort for people with sensitive teeth or gums.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High levels of fruit acids can irritate the stomach if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar can be eaten straight from the package for a quick energy boost. It can also be sliced and added to smoothies, yogurt, or oatmeal to enhance flavor. If a softer texture is preferred, let the bar thaw slightly before consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bars in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once removed from the package, consume within 2–3 days for optimal texture and taste. Do not keep the thawed product at room temperature for more than 30 minutes.

content.title: About
content.content: Restructured potato chips are a dry snack made from potato puree that is shaped into thin sheets and fried until crisp. A light salt seasoning provides a subtle salty taste without overwhelming the natural potato flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Restructured chips differ from traditional ones because their base is potato puree rather than whole potato slices.
A modest amount of salt enhances the natural potato taste while keeping the snack less salty overall.
The production process can utilize potato off‑cuts, improving raw material efficiency.
In many markets these chips are sold in 50–150 g packages.
Their thin texture is achieved by rapid high‑temperature frying.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Potato chips provide carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: A small amount of vitamin C survives the quick frying, supporting the immune system.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, important for fluid balance and heart function.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When produced correctly, these chips contain no trans fats, making them less harmful than some other snack foods.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Chips are calorie‑dense, so they should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Even a light salt level should be considered by individuals monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may have an allergic reaction to potato.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the chips as a standalone snack, add them to salads, use as a crunchy topping for soups, or incorporate into dishes for textural contrast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store chips in an airtight package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep them refrigerated to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑sodium canned chicken soup is a ready‑to‑eat soup made from chicken meat, vegetables, and aromatic herbs. The lower salt content makes it suitable for people monitoring their sodium intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The quick heat‑treatment process preserves most of the soup’s nutrients.
Sodium reduction is achieved by replacing part of the salt with herbs and natural flavor enhancers.
The chicken broth is often prepared from bones, increasing collagen content.
The product has a long shelf life without refrigeration.
Metal cans protect the soup from light and oxygen, extending freshness.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Reduced salt helps maintain normal blood pressure for those limiting sodium.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup contains vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: A warm broth contributes to fluid balance in the body.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Warm soup is gentle on the digestive system, making it suitable for people with reduced appetite.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to chicken protein should avoid this product.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some canned soups may contain additives such as sulfites, which can trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Higher fat content in broth
items.content: Certain recipes include added fat, which should be considered in low‑fat diets.

items.title: Can material
items.content: Improperly coated cans could leach trace metals; reputable brands follow safety standards.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the can in a saucepan or microwave until boiling. Optionally stir in fresh vegetables, herbs, or noodles. Serve hot as a standalone meal or as a starter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer leftovers to an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Pumpkin soup is a thick, aromatic soup made from fresh or canned pumpkin, broth, cream, and spices. The pumpkin gives a gentle sweet flavor, while the cream creates a velvety texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pumpkin is one of the oldest cultivated plants, grown by humans for over 7,000 years.
Pumpkin soup is traditionally served in autumn and winter because pumpkin is rich in vitamins that support immunity in cold weather.
In some countries, such as the United States, pumpkin soup is often garnished with pumpkin seeds and croutons.
Pumpkin belongs to the Cucurbitaceae family, along with cucumbers, zucchini, and watermelons.
There are many recipe variations, from classic creamy versions to vegan ones made with coconut milk.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Pumpkin provides a high amount of beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in pumpkin soup helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: When made with a moderate amount of cream, pumpkin soup can be a light dish suitable for weight management.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Pumpkin contains antioxidants such as vitamin E and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Pumpkin allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to pumpkin.

items.title: Added sugar in canned pumpkin
items.content: Canned pumpkin sometimes contains added sugar, which may be undesirable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Pumpkin contains oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pumpkin soup is served hot, often topped with a swirl of cream, pumpkin seeds, herbs, or croutons. It can be prepared as a smooth purée or a lighter version without cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared soup in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze it in portion‑size bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to a boil before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Tamale, no meat is a traditional Mexican dish made from corn masa dough and a filling of vegetables, beans, cheese and spices, wrapped in corn husks (or banana leaves) and steamed until cooked. It has a gentle corn aroma, a slightly sweet base flavor and a rich, savory spice profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tamales are among the oldest dishes in the Americas, prepared by the Maya and Aztec civilizations.
They are traditionally served at celebrations and holidays, especially Day of the Dead and Christmas.
Corn husks used for wrapping impart a distinctive aroma and keep the tamale shape during steaming.
There are countless regional variations, from sweet fruit‑filled to spicy chili‑and‑cheese versions.
The vegetarian, meat‑free version has gained popularity in recent decades with the rise of plant‑based diets.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Corn masa provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Tamales deliver slowly digestible carbohydrates that help maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain thiamine, niacin and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Plant protein
items.content: Beans and cheese in the filling supply a complete set of essential amino acids for vegetarians.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Corn and vegetables contain carotenoids and vitamin C, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Fillings seasoned with soy sauce or salty cheeses can be high in salt.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Tamales are moderately calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: If not cooled promptly, steamed tamales can spoil quickly; they should be refrigerated within two hours of cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tamales are typically served hot, unwrapped from the corn husk. Eat them as a main dish or with salsa, guacamole, or sour cream. For a fresh touch, add chopped cilantro, lime juice, and sliced avocado.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked tamales in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a freezer‑safe bag; reheat by steaming for 10‑15 minutes or microwaving with a splash of water.

turkey-or-chicken-burger-on-wheat-bun.title: Turkey or Chicken Burger on Wheat Bun

content.title: About
content.content: A turkey or chicken burger is a lean patty made from ground turkey or chicken meat, served on a soft wheat bun. It is low in fat, high in protein, and often chosen for healthier meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is considered a leaner meat than beef and is popular in diet-friendly dishes.
Chicken provides all essential amino acids needed by the body.
A wheat bun adds a subtle sweetness and a tender texture to the burger.
The burger can be grilled, pan‑fried, or baked while keeping the patty juicy.
In some cultures turkey is referred to as “dark meat” despite its light color.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Ground turkey or chicken delivers a high‑quality protein that supports muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, poultry contains less saturated fat, which is better for heart health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry meat is abundant in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: The patty provides iron, zinc, and phosphorus, which are vital for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: Protein and zinc in turkey or chicken help strengthen the body’s immune response.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird meat.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw poultry can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; the burger must be cooked thoroughly.

items.title: Sodium in the bun
items.content: Wheat buns often contain added salt, which should be limited by people with high blood pressure.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The wheat bun contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the burger hot, typically with lettuce, tomato, cucumber, and a light sauce such as yogurt‑based dressing or mustard. Avocado or cheese can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked burger refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 2 days. It can be frozen for up to 3 months. Store the bun in a dry place to prevent it from becoming soggy.
